passages.t: Uzziah seeks God and becomes powerful
passages.happening:
The people of Judah make sixteen-year-old Uzziah king (verse 1). He rebuilds Eloth and restores it to Judah (verse 2) and reigns fifty-two years. ‘He sought God throughout the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God. And as long as he sought the LORD, God gave him success’ (verse 5).

He wins wars against the Philistines, the Arabs and the Meunites, and the Ammonites bring tribute (verses 6-8). He builds towers in Jerusalem and in the wilderness, digs cisterns, and keeps herds and vineyards, ‘since he was a lover of the soil’ (verse 10). He has a trained army and equips it with shields, spears, helmets and armor (verses 11-14). ‘And in Jerusalem he made skillfully designed devices to shoot arrows and catapult large stones from the towers and corners. So his fame spread far and wide, for he was helped tremendously so that he became powerful’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Uzziah, called Azariah in 2 Kings, begins well and ends badly, like Joash and Amaziah before him. His early reign is the most prosperous since Solomon. His fifty-two years likely include a time beside his father at the start and beside his son Jotham at the end; a common reconstruction puts him about 792 to 740 BC. It was a time of prosperity for Judah and for Israel under Jeroboam the Second, because Assyria was briefly weak and Aram had been pushed back. Amos and Hosea date their work partly to his reign, and Amos mentions an earthquake in his day that was remembered for centuries.

The chapter gives his achievements generously, because in Chronicles success is what God gives to those who seek him. Eloth on the Gulf of Aqaba gave Judah access to Red Sea trade. The skillfully designed devices are often translated as machines for shooting arrows and stones; some scholars think they were defensive screens on the towers, since true catapults are not otherwise attested until centuries later.

The first half ends on the words he became powerful, framed by two notes that God helped him. Who to notice: Zechariah, who taught him the fear of God. As long as Uzziah sought the LORD, he prospered.
passages.later: Amos dates his words ‘two years before the earthquake’ (Amos 1:1), and Zechariah remembered ‘the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah’ (Zechariah 14:5).
passages.asks: Uzziah sought God in the days of a good teacher. Ask who taught you the fear of God, and whether you still seek him as you did then. And ask what strength God has given you that could become a danger.

passages.t: Pride, incense, and a king cut off
passages.happening:
‘But when Uzziah grew powerful, his arrogance led to his own destruction. He was unfaithful to the LORD his God, for he entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the altar of incense’ (verse 16). Azariah the priest and eighty brave priests go in after him (verse 17) and say, “Uzziah, you have no right to offer incense to the LORD. Only the priests, the descendants of Aaron, are consecrated to burn incense” (verse 18).

Uzziah, censer in hand, rages at the priests, and a skin disease breaks out on his forehead before the altar (verse 19). The priests rush him out, ‘Indeed, he himself hurried to get out, because the LORD had afflicted him’ (verse 20). ‘So King Uzziah was a leper until the day of his death. He lived in isolation, leprous and cut off from the house of the LORD, while his son Jotham had charge of the royal palace to govern the people of the land’ (verse 21). He is buried in a field near the royal tombs, because the people said that he was a leper (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The second half begins by turning the same word from gift to snare: when Uzziah grew powerful. His heart was lifted up, gavah, the word used well of Jehoshaphat and badly here. He was unfaithful, ma'al, the Chronicler's word for sacrilege against what belongs to God.

In Israel kingship and priesthood were separated by law. Burning incense on the golden altar was the task of Aaron's descendants, and Numbers tells how Korah's company perished when they claimed that right. Many neighboring kings served as chief priests of their gods, so Uzziah's act would have looked natural in the world around him. In Israel it was a trespass against holiness.

The word translated leprosy, tsara, covered a range of skin diseases, not only the condition now called Hansen's disease. The law made a person with it ritually unclean and required them to live apart, which is why Uzziah was cut off from the house of the LORD; the house of separateness in verse 21 names where he lived. Kings says only that the LORD struck him and that he lived in a separate house while Jotham governed; Chronicles gives the reason. A stone plaque in Aramaic from the late Second Temple period, found in Jerusalem and now in the Israel Museum, says that the bones of Uzziah king of Judah were brought there and must not be opened, so his remains were reburied long after his death.

The text tells this as God's judgment on one king's defiant act in the temple, after a warning he raged against. It is not a key for reading anyone's illness.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: Isaiah's call came at the end of this reign: ‘In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted; and the train of His robe filled the temple’ (Isaiah 6:1).
passages.hard:
Wasn't a lifelong skin disease an excessive punishment for burning incense?

To a modern reader, burning incense can look like a harmless act of devotion. The chapter frames it differently. Uzziah was warned by eighty priests, told plainly he had no right, and answered with rage, so the act was deliberate defiance of God's order, not an honest mistake. In Israel's worship, access to God's presence was a matter of life and death; the deaths of Aaron's sons and of Korah's company stand behind this scene. Some readers note that the judgment fits the offense: the king who pushed into the holy place is barred from it. Others find the severity hard and say honestly that Chronicles presents God's holiness as more dangerous than modern readers are used to. Both responses take the text seriously.
passages.asks: Uzziah reached for a place God had not given him, and lost the place he had. Ask where your success has made you think the rules no longer apply to you. And ask how you answer when someone tells you, You have no right.
